title: Chai Spice Is Officially America's Second-Biggest Flavour Trend — And India's Pantry Is Driving the Revolution
excerpt: A major industry report ranks chai spice as the number two flavour trend in North America for 2026, as cardamom, ginger, and clove conquer categories from ice cream to protein bars.
body:
For decades, chai in America meant one thing: a syrupy, milk-heavy latte from a coffee chain, bearing only a passing resemblance to the masala chai that fuels mornings across the subcontinent. But something has shifted. In 2026, chai spice is not just a beverage flavour. It is the second-biggest flavour trend in all of North American food and drink, according to a major new report from IFF, one of the world's largest flavour and fragrance companies.

The ranking, which placed chai behind only tiramisu in IFF's annual trend predictions, reflects a dramatic expansion of Indian spice profiles into categories that would have seemed improbable a few years ago: protein shakes, cereal bars, confectionery, frozen desserts, flavoured milks, and savory-sweet snacks.

## Beyond the Latte

IFF's report describes chai spice as "warm, aromatic, and globally rooted," noting that its blend of black tea, cinnamon, clove, ginger, and cardamom delivers "approachable global flavor with a wellness-adjacent halo." The company predicts continued innovation in what it calls "dirty chai" beverages, chai-spiced chocolates, cardamom-forward variations, and savory-sweet snack applications.

This tracks with what is already visible on American shelves and menus. Iced specialty teas are now on 4.2 percent of US restaurant menus, up more than 16 percent year over year, according to Technomic's Ignite menu database. Matcha has grown nearly 25 percent. But chai's expansion is notable for its breadth — it is moving beyond tea and coffee into food categories where Indian spice profiles have historically had little presence.

The wellness dimension is a significant accelerant. Cardamom, ginger, and clove — the backbone of any good masala chai — carry established health associations in both Ayurvedic and Western nutritional traditions. As functional foods and "better-for-you" formulations continue to dominate consumer preferences, chai spice offers brands a flavour profile that tastes indulgent while signalling wellness.

## India's Pantry Goes Mainstream

The chai trend does not exist in isolation. It sits alongside the broader mainstreaming of Indian pantry staples in American food culture. Turmeric was named 2026's Herb of the Year by the International Herb Association. Ghee has become a fixture in Whole Foods and Trader Joe's. Indian grocery chains like Patel Brothers are expanding aggressively across the country. And brands like VAHDAM India are building direct-to-consumer businesses that bypass the traditional spice import supply chain entirely.

What is new in 2026 is the scale of the crossover. Truly Indian, a brand of ADF Foods, was named a NEXTY Awards finalist in two categories at Natural Products Expo West this year for its Tikka Masala Naan and Crispy Chili Mango Chutney. The awards, which recognise innovation in natural products, signal that Indian flavours are no longer a niche ethnic aisle phenomenon but a mainstream grocery category competing head-to-head with Italian, Mexican, and Asian-fusion products.

## What NRIs Should Know

For Indians in the diaspora, the chai spice trend carries a familiar mix of pride and mild exasperation. On one hand, it is validating to see the flavours of home embraced at industrial scale. On the other, there is the perennial question of whether mainstream adoption dilutes or distorts the original.

The answer, increasingly, is that it does both — and that this is not necessarily a bad thing. The chai-spiced protein bar at Trader Joe's is not your grandmother's kadak chai. But it is a gateway product that normalises Indian flavours for tens of millions of American consumers, many of whom will then seek out the real thing. And for Indian food brands seeking shelf space, the trend represents an enormous commercial opportunity.

IFF's trend report also highlights "sweet heat" — the pairing of sweetness with layered spice — as the third-biggest trend for 2026, another profile deeply rooted in Indian culinary traditions. Taken together, the top three trends for this year read like a love letter to the flavours of the subcontinent, even if the packaging would be unrecognisable in a Mumbai kitchen.

## What Is Next

The chai spice trend shows no signs of plateauing. Industry analysts expect continued innovation in ready-to-drink chai formats, chai-flavoured dairy and dairy-alternative products, and seasonal chai launches timed to the autumn and winter months when warm spice profiles see peak demand. For Indian food entrepreneurs and brands, the message is clear: America's palate has arrived at your doorstep. The question is no longer whether Indian flavours can go mainstream. It is which ones are next.
author: Diaspora Desk
